div.font: Appendix D (1/5)
Purpose, Explanation, and Arbitrariness

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 796px; height: 1px; padding-top: 493px; margin-left: 28px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;

b.style: font-size: 12px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.font: - What something is for - the "why" something matters, in the sense of its direction, goal, or intended end
- 2 possible meanings:

- Phenomenological/Intentional: the "end"/"direction" that is defined by your "aim" (ex. I reach for a cup "to drink water", I bake a cake "to feed guests", etc.)
- Non-Phenomenological/Functional: the "end"/"direction" that is not defined by your "aim" (ex. this key is "for that lock", this cake is "to be eaten", etc.)
- An answer to "why" (ie. the "what" of purpose) or "how" (ie. a causal chain of "why"s)
- 3 possible meanings:

- Causal: what is the cause?
- Intentional: what is someone's goal (ie. their will/aim)?
- Rule/pattern-based: what rule/pattern fits this behavior?
- An unavoidable pull; where X can't occur without Y
- 5 possible meanings:
1 - Survival: "X needs Y to survive (or exist)"

div.span: : without X, I won't feel comfort or assurance

div.font: 3 - Causal: given X, Y will occur regardless (whether you want it or not) - or, Y cannot occur unless X occurs
4 - Explanatory: to finish answering a question (ie. "if we stop here, the question isn't answered")
5 - Methodological: [logical] consistency is not achieved unless the rules/standards are followed (ie. "if the rules aren't followed, the conclusion is not valid")
- Lacking purpose
- 7 possible meanings:
1 - Subjective/Preference/Whim: something that occurs because of preference, not an external standard (ex. "I painted my room green because I like it")
2 - Accidental/Uncaused/Meaningless: something that lacks both preference and an external standard

div.span: 3 - Lack of Integrity/Principle/Consistency: ad hoc rescue; falsely changing the rules (when confronted with a contradiction) in order to protect a claim

div.font: 4 - Lack of Explanation: something that lacks an answer to explain its behavior

u.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

font.span: 5 - Unpredictable: when outcomes consistently do not align with expectations with certainty (ex. the outcome of a coin toss, with certainty)
6 - Lack of Pattern/Undefinable: when there is no greater identifiable pattern or connection (ex. static noise)

b.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

span.style: background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255)); font-size: 11px;

display: inline-block; font-size: 1px; font-family: Helvetica; color: #000000; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;
div.span: The word "arbitrary" feels obvious, but it quietly carries multiple meanings in real arguments. The same is true of need (as in, “this needs an explanation”) and purpose (as in, “this has no purpose”). When these meanings aren’t made explicit,
words can keep their emotional familiarity while losing fixed meaning - allowing arguments to
borrow the emotional/intuitive force of an “obvious” word without earning it rationally - making claims sound stronger than they really are. The
same term can be heard one way and used another way
, people can end up disagreeing while talking past each other, and listeners may agree with a version of the claim the speaker never actually defended.
It gives [phenomenologically] grounded definitions for the relevant meanings of "purpose", "explanation", "need", and "arbitrary" (with examples as needed).
It shows how common objections to the project use these terms, what they implicitly commit to, and how those commitments are addressed by the project’s results.

switch.text: The word "arbitrary" feels obvious, but it quietly carries multiple meanings in real arguments. The same is true of need (as in, “this needs an explanation”) and purpose (as in, “this has no purpose”). When these meanings aren’t made explicit, words can keep their emotional familiarity while losing fixed meaning - allowing arguments to borrow the emotional/intuitive force of an “obvious” word without earning it rationally - making claims sound stronger than they really are. The same term can be heard one way and used another way, people can end up disagreeing while talking past each other, and listeners may agree with a version of the claim the speaker never actually defended....

div.style: display: flex; align-items: unsafe flex-start; justify-content: unsafe flex-start; width: 796px; height: 1px; padding-top: 273px; margin-left: 28px;
box-sizing: border-box; font-size: 0; text-align: left; color: #000000;
display: inline-block; font-size: 1px; font-family: Helvetica; color: #000000; line-height: 1.2; pointer-events: all; white-space: normal; word-wrap: normal;

div.span: Before assessing any claim or argument, we need to ensure our definitions are explicit and sound - and to define anything, we need to make sure that all terms are properly grounded [phenomenologically].

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

b.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: when its meaning is traceable to something we can directly recognize in experience [phenomenologically], such as "ouch", "trying", "remembering", "seeing", "being surprised", "resistance", "effort", "up", and so on.

But many of the words we use in arguments are not referring to these "internal" experiences. Rather, they refer to the "external" side of experience - things we don't access [phenomenologically], but can still recognize by how they show up to us.

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: So, an external term is grounded when its meaning is traceable to a stable feature of experience that we can also point to, such as "independence from my will" (things that occur whether I want to or not), "regularity" (it always or often happens the same way), "dependence" (one thing always follows another), and so on.

span.style: font-size: 11px; background-color: transparent; color: light-dark(rgb(0, 0, 0), rgb(255, 255, 255));

div.span: With that grounding in place, we can now define the key terms used in common objections - so that each definition stays traceable to what it is meant to refer to, disagreements become precise and clear to everyone, and meaning can be grounded in a way that anyone can understand.
